name: stri_length
title: Count the Number of Code Points

origin.description: Count the Unicode code points in each string.

arguments.name: str
arguments.text: A character vector, or an object coerced to character.

origin.details: The count is code points, not the number of columns used when the string is printed. A missing string stays missing. An ill-formed UTF-8 string is an error. A byte encoding is an error.
origin.value: An integer vector the same length as str.
origin.example:
x <- stri_length(c("abc", NA))
cat(paste0("stri_length(c(\"abc\", NA)) returns ", paste(ifelse(is.na(x), "NA", x), collapse = ", "), ".\n"))

translation.description: Count the Unicode code points in each string.

arguments.name: str
arguments.text: A string, NA, a number, a complex value, or a list of those. None is an empty vector.

translation.details: len of a Python string is the code-point count. A list is promoted the way R's c() promotes a mixed vector, then each value is coerced with as.character. An integer in the R integer range is printed in decimal. A double uses 15 significant digits and scientific notation when that form is shorter. NA stays missing. The string "NA" has length 2.
translation.value: An int, or NA. A list or tuple returns a list. None returns an empty list.
translation.example:
from stringi.length import stri_length
from stringi._na import NA
x = stri_length(["abc", NA])
shown = ", ".join("NA" if value is NA else str(value) for value in x)
print(f"stri_length([\"abc\", NA]) returns {shown}.")
